title: Ground-up green industrialization: Africa’s informal economy as a neglected learning ecosystem
body:
It is no longer news that Africa’s informal (repair, scrap and recycle) economy holds immense potential for a "ground-up" green industrialization. This has been the focus of a few Policy Insights on this platform.

But what if it offers something deeper? What if Africa’s informal economy is not just a starting point but a fully functioning learning ecosystem that we can LEARN from, LEVERAGE, and SCALE?

Just look closely! In scrap metal markets, plastic recovery networks, e-waste clusters, and repair sectors across African economies, we see continuous, practice-based industrial learning.

Workers in this ecosystem aren’t waiting for formal training or policy support. They learn by dismantling, repairing, and recovering value from what others discard.

In Nigeria, for instance, it is uncommon to find a roadside mechanic without formal engineering education diagnosing complex engine faults, improvising tools, and restoring functionality under severe constraints.

This is not improvisation born out of necessity alone. It is capability formation in action where actors within systems accumulate deep, experience-based knowledge in:

- how to identify and separate valuable materials
- how to extend the life of products through repair and refurbishment
- how to adapt tools and techniques to local conditions
- how to operate efficient, low-cost recovery and recycling processes

**Implication:** Africa’s informal economy is already doing what any successful industrial system must do: learn, adapt, and upgrade continuously.

Two things make this unique:

- the learning is at its most organic: distributed, practice-based, and deeply embedded in local realities
- it is also happening in a decentralized, highly resilient manner, mostly without policy support, infrastructure, or formal recognition

At a time when formal industrial systems in many African countries remain fragmented, this implies that the informal economy may well be the continent’s largest and most functional industrial learning platform.

Yet conversations often treat the sector as a problem to be eliminated, rather than a system to be strengthened.

This is a strategic mistake and calls for a rethink.

If we take the idea of the informal economy as a learning system seriously, three shifts become urgent: LEARN from it and not just regulate it. LEVERAGE it as a foundation for green capabilities. SCALE it from survival to industrial transformation.

**Bottom line:** Africa’s learning economy, requisite for green industrialization, isn’t starting from zero. It already has one hidden in plain sight. It has millions of people learning, adapting, and innovating every day under conditions that demand efficiency, creativity, and resilience.

The real question is how the continent can learn, leverage, and scale what it already knows how to do.
